# A Place to Sit

On the morning the bench disappeared, Ada arrived seven minutes early and had nowhere to put her anger.

Usually she sat on it.

The bench stood outside the old post office, beneath a plane tree that shed bark in thin, pale plates. Its wooden slats had been painted green so many times that the paint had softened their edges. One of the iron legs resembled a lion’s paw, though the other three did not. Nobody knew whether this was intentional.

Ada had been sitting there every Tuesday for eleven years, waiting for the number sixteen bus.

Now there were four pale rectangles on the pavement.

She examined them with the attention usually reserved for footprints at a crime scene. Then she looked up and down the street, as if the bench might have wandered a short distance and become confused.

The bus arrived.

“Bench has gone,” she told the driver.

“Morning to you too.”

“Did you see who took it?”

“I’m more concerned with people taking buses.”

Ada boarded, but she did not consider the matter closed.

***

At home she telephoned the council.

The first person transferred her to Street Furniture. Street Furniture transferred her to Public Realm. Public Realm explained that seating fell under Assets, unless it was commemorative seating, in which case she wanted Parks.

“There’s no plaque,” Ada said.

“Are you certain?”

“I’ve had eleven years to read it.”

Assets asked for an asset number.

“It was a bench.”

“Yes, but which bench?”

“The one that isn’t there.”

There was a silence in which Ada could hear somebody opening a packet of crisps.

Eventually a young man named Lewis agreed to investigate. He sounded tired in a way she associated with people who had recently begun working for a living and already suspected an administrative error.

“Could you describe its condition?” he asked.

“Absent.”

“Before that.”

Ada considered.

“It wobbled if someone large sat on the left.”

Lewis typed something.

“And the surface?”

“Green.”

“Was there exposed timber?”

“It was a wooden bench. I hope so.”

He promised to call back.

Ada wrote his name on the pad beside the telephone. Underneath it she wrote BENCH, pressing hard enough to leave an impression on the next three pages.

Her daughter called that evening.

“What have you been doing?”

“Trying to find some furniture.”

“Are you finally replacing that armchair?”

“No.”

“The spring is coming through.”

“It knows where I sit.”

Her daughter lived four hours away and had developed a habit of treating everything in Ada’s house as a warning. The armchair was a warning. The stairs were a warning. A jar of marmalade with a stubborn lid was practically a medical event.

Ada did not mention the bench again.

She knew how the story would sound: an old woman becoming upset about a minor alteration to a street. She had heard such stories herself, and had not always been patient with them.

***

Lewis called on Thursday.

“The bench was removed following a condition assessment.”

“By whom?”

“A contractor.”

“What condition did they assess?”

“There was a structural concern.”

“What concern?”

“I don’t have the full report.”

“Where is it now?”

“The report?”

“The bench, Lewis.”

He said he would find out.

Meanwhile, Ada began asking questions.

The newsagent had seen a flatbed truck at half past six. The woman who swept the post office steps had assumed the bench was being repainted. A cyclist claimed it had been dangerous for years, though under questioning he admitted he had never sat on it.

At the pharmacy, Ada found an ally.

“Mrs. Bell used that bench,” the assistant said. “She could get here from her flat if she rested halfway.”

“Where does she rest now?”

“She doesn’t come. Her neighbour collects.”

Ada bought a notebook.

On the first page she wrote: WHO SAT THERE?

She disliked petitions. People signed them to get you off the doorstep, and then you were left with a damp clipboard and the illusion of support. She wanted particulars.

She learned that the kitchen porter from the hotel ate his evening meal there before catching the bus home. His staff meal came in a plastic tub. He preferred to eat outside because the hotel basement smelled of hot laundry.

Two schoolgirls waited there for one girl’s grandfather, who was always late and always brought a dog.

A man from the betting shop used the bench because his wife believed he had stopped smoking.

“I’m not putting that in the notebook,” Ada told him.

“Much appreciated.”

There was a courier who changed his socks there when it rained.

There was a woman who had once sat down crying and been offered a satsuma by a stranger.

There was a stranger who remembered offering a satsuma and had worried ever since that it was an absurd thing to do.

Ada found these last two separately, which pleased her.

By Sunday she had filled nine pages.

She also discovered that almost nobody knew anybody else’s name. They described one another by coats, dogs, shopping bags, times of day.

“The tall one with the careful shoes.”

“The fellow whose dog sits on his feet.”

“That woman who laughs before answering the phone.”

The bench had apparently been running a modest neighbourhood without informing the authorities.

***

Lewis arrived the following Tuesday wearing a council lanyard and shoes too thin for the weather.

Ada was standing beside the pale rectangles.

“You came,” she said.

“I had another site visit nearby.”

She let him have this.

He carried a tablet, which he consulted before looking at the pavement.

“The support brackets were corroded.”

“Could they have been repaired?”

“Possibly.”

“Then why weren’t they?”

“It may not have been economical.”

“Compared with what?”

He shifted the tablet into his other hand.

Ada had spent thirty-four years ordering stock for a hospital kitchen. She knew that “not economical” sometimes meant a thing had been carefully costed. At other times it meant nobody wanted to telephone a welder.

Lewis explained that the bench had entered the system as a removal rather than a replacement.

“How does it become a replacement?”

“A request has to be raised.”

“Consider it raised.”

“There’s a process.”

“I’m beginning to admire its stamina.”

He smiled despite himself.

She showed him the notebook.

At first he read it with the expression of a man being handed evidence of somebody else’s enthusiasm. Then he slowed down.

“Mrs. Bell,” he said. “Is that the woman in the flats on Mercer Street?”

“You know her?”

“My gran knows her.”

“Your gran probably knows everyone.”

“She makes a serious effort.”

He read another page.

Ada watched a bus pull in. A woman carrying two bags paused near the tree, looked at the empty pavement, then leaned against the post office wall.

Lewis saw her too.

“There might be a small accessibility budget,” he said.

“Would that buy a bench?”

“It might buy part of one.”

“Which part?”

He laughed, then caught himself.

“I’ll see what I can do.”

Before leaving, he crouched to photograph the old fixing holes. His trouser cuff touched a puddle, and he stood up with a dark crescent around one ankle.

Ada felt a small, unexpected sympathy for him.

When she had been his age, she too had imagined that doing a job meant being allowed to do it.

***

The replacement proposal arrived three weeks later.

It showed a silver bench with three separate seats divided by metal bars. It looked like equipment for testing obedience.

Ada telephoned Lewis.

“Why are there fences on it?”

“Armrests.”

“Between every person?”

“They help people stand.”

“So do ordinary armrests.”

“It’s a standard approved model.”

“Can you sit next to someone?”

“Yes.”

“Comfortably?”

“That depends on the people.”

She studied the drawing again.

The old bench had held four adults when necessary, or three adults and a child whose feet stuck straight out. This one permitted exactly three people, each in an assigned territory.

“Is there another model?”

“There are several.”

“Send them.”

There were twelve. Some had no backs. Some were made of perforated metal. One was described as a perch and seemed designed by someone morally opposed to sitting.

Ada made tea.

She laid the printed pages across her kitchen table, moving a bowl of oranges to the windowsill. Then she called Mrs. Bell.

They had met twice by then. Mrs. Bell possessed a walking stick, a sharp laugh, and extensive opinions about the paving outside the chemist.

“Come and look at something,” Ada said.

“I can’t walk that far.”

“I’ll get you a taxi.”

“That seems extravagant.”

“Yes,” Ada said. “It’s a very important bench.”

Mrs. Bell arrived wearing lipstick and carrying biscuits.

They chose a wooden model with a back, end supports, and one central armrest. It was not beautiful, but it looked willing.

Then they discussed placement.

The drawing put the bench directly beneath the tree.

“Birds,” Mrs. Bell said.

They moved it a little to the right.

The new position faced the road.

“Nothing to look at,” Ada said.

They angled it toward the post office doors and the corner where people appeared from the market.

For twenty minutes they debated the winter sun.

Neither had expected to spend an afternoon designing somewhere to sit. By the time the taxi came, the biscuit plate was empty and the oranges were back on the table.

***

In April, the project stalled.

The pavement belonged to Highways. The tree pit belonged to Parks. The old post office was privately owned, and the proposed bench position might interfere with an access route that nobody had used since the building’s side entrance was bricked up in 1987.

Lewis sent an apologetic email.

Ada went to the library and asked for old street photographs.

The librarian, who loved a question with edges, produced local history books, archived planning documents, and a photograph of the post office opening ceremony.

There was the mayor, wearing a chain large enough to anchor a boat.

There were children holding flags.

And there was the bench.

It had originally stood farther from the tree, almost exactly where Ada and Mrs. Bell wanted the new one.

The photograph was dated 1954.

Ada turned it over, though of course there was nothing on the back except a library stamp.

She had been seven then.

Her mother might have walked past that ceremony. Her father might have complained about the traffic. The bench had existed through all the years when Ada had been too busy to notice benches: school, work, marriage, babies, her husband’s long illness, the bewildering paperwork afterward.

She took a copy to the council office.

Lewis came downstairs.

“I’m not sure historical placement establishes current permission,” he said.

“No,” Ada replied. “But it establishes that the world did not collapse.”

He pinned the photograph above his desk.

She knew because he sent her a picture.

Later that week, he found a retired highways officer who remembered the bricked-up entrance. The officer found a reference number. The reference number led to a document. The document established that the access route had ceased to be an access route thirty-six years earlier.

The permission took two more weeks.

During this time, the plane tree opened its leaves.

***

The bench arrived on a Monday, which Ada considered inconsiderate.

Lewis called at ten.

“They’re installing it now.”

She put on her coat over her gardening clothes and went out with soil still beneath her nails.

Two workers were unloading wooden slats. A third was measuring the pavement.

The new bench was lighter than the old one, honey-coloured rather than green. Its supports were plain. None resembled a lion’s paw.

Ada felt, to her annoyance, disappointed.

After all that work, she had wanted the lost thing returned, not replaced by a reasonable alternative.

One worker glanced up.

“You the bench lady?”

“Apparently.”

“Where do you want it?”

She pointed.

He checked the plan.

“That’s where it says.”

“I’m glad we agree.”

By noon it was bolted down.

There was no ceremony. The workers collected their tools and left behind a little pale dust, which one of them swept into a pan.

Ada stood looking at the finished bench.

“Go on,” Lewis said.

He had come over during his lunch break with a sandwich still in its packet.

“You first,” she said.

“I’ve got to get back.”

“So have I.”

Neither moved.

Then Mrs. Bell appeared around the corner, walking slowly with her stick.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake,” she said.

She lowered herself onto the bench, tested the central armrest, and shifted until she was comfortable.

“Yes,” she said. “That’ll do.”

Ada sat beside her.

Lewis took a photograph for the project record, being careful to ask permission first. Mrs. Bell told him to wait while she straightened her collar.

***

By June, the wood had lost its raw brightness. Someone spilled coffee. A child drew a tiny blue star beneath one armrest, invisible unless you bent down. The hotel porter returned with his plastic tub.

Ada still caught the Tuesday bus, though sometimes she let one pass.

She had begun meeting Mrs. Bell there on Fridays. They discussed groceries and occasionally people. Neither called it an arrangement.

One afternoon, a man lowered himself onto the far end with a sigh.

“Good to have this,” he said.

“Yes,” Ada replied.

“Council finally did something useful.”

She considered explaining about Lewis, the notebook, the photographs, the biscuits, and the retired highways officer.

Instead she watched a girl waiting at the crossing, holding a dog’s lead in one hand and two ice creams in the other.

“Yes,” she said again.

The man leaned back and closed his eyes.

Ada moved her shopping bag to give him a little more room.
